handsOnLab.brief: You will provenance-check a model artifact the way you would before letting it near production: hash it, document it in an ML-BOM, write a vendor-style evaluation checklist, and practice the deny-by-default decision on an unprovenanced file.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Re-running sha256sum reproduces the recorded hash exactly; every ML-BOM field is filled with a real value (no 'TBD'); the checklist contains your own pass/fail verdict with reasons.
handsOnLab.deliverable: ml-bom.json (complete ML bill of materials) + provenance-checklist.md (hash record, verification steps, vendor-claim evaluation, deploy/refuse verdict).
steps: Create a working directory ~/il29-m25-lab and inside it a stand-in artifact: python3 -c "open('demo-model.bin','wb').write(b'MODEL-ARTIFACT-STANDIN-v1.0')". In production this would be the real weights file.
Compute its SHA-256: sha256sum demo-model.bin and record the digest. This is the provenance anchor — any bit flip changes it.
Write a model card (model-card.md): intended use, training data description, eval summary, limitations, and a 'do not use for' section. Keep it honest and short.

Draft ml-bom.json with fields: artifact_name, artifact_sha256 (paste the real digest), base_model, training_data_sources (with per-source hashes or 'unverified'), preprocessing_code_version, hyperparameters, eval_results (precision/recall at threshold), licenses, known_limitations.

Simulate the untrusted-download case: create evil-model.bin with different bytes, note that its hash differs, and write the refuse verdict in the checklist with the reason (no provenance, no signature).

Write provenance-checklist.md: the exact verification commands you ran, where a real hash/signature would be fetched out-of-band, and the five vendor questions from the notes with your answers for this artifact.
Add a 'vendor claim evaluation' section: invent a plausible-sounding vendor claim for this artifact (e.g. '99.9% accurate'), then demolish it with the accuracy-vs-recall arithmetic from the notes.
Re-run sha256sum on demo-model.bin and confirm the digest matches ml-bom.json byte-for-byte.
Review the full ml-bom.json: every field must contain a real value. Any field you cannot fill honestly is a supply-chain gap — document it as one.
Read both files end to end and confirm a stranger could reproduce your verification from the checklist alone.
handsOnLab.title: Provenance-check and document a model artifact

choices: Load it in a sandbox VM — sandboxes make untrusted code safe enough
Check the file extension; .pt files are just weights and cannot execute code
Refuse it: no provenance, no hash, no signature — unprovenanced artifacts do not enter the environment
Load it only on your workstation, not a server, to limit blast radius
mockTask.explain: Deny-by-default applies to models: without provenance you cannot establish what the artifact is, and deserialization formats can execute code. A sandbox reduces but does not remove the risk, and extension-sniffing is not a security control.
mockTask.q: Panel question: a teammate found a pre-trained malware classifier on a forum and wants to torch.load it to 'save training time' before the Oct 13 go-live. What is your call?

notes.body:
Every AI system you deploy is a supply chain, and every link you did not build yourself is a trust decision. Walk the chain for a typical security model — say, a phishing-email classifier. Someone collected the emails (were they representative? poisoned?). Someone labeled them (by hand? by a heuristic? by an outsourced team?). Someone wrote the preprocessing (does it strip the exact header fields the attacker will manipulate?). Someone chose a base model (which checkpoint, from where, with what hash?). Someone packaged it (pickle? a safe format?). Someone hosts the download (their server? a mirror? a forum link?). And at inference time it runs inside your dependency stack (which PyTorch build? which CUDA driver? which container base image?). A compromise at any one of these points changes what the model does, and unlike a compromised binary, a compromised model fails in ways that look like ordinary mistakes — slightly worse accuracy on exactly the attacker's inputs. That is what makes AI supply-chain attacks insidious: there is no crash, no obvious malware, just a model that quietly does the attacker's bidding on trigger inputs while behaving normally on everything else. Your job as the operator is to enumerate this chain for every model you touch and demand evidence at each link: hashes for artifacts, signatures for origin, version pins for dependencies, provenance records for data. Where evidence is missing, you do not have a supply chain — you have a hope chain. Worked example: a teammate drops a malware-classifier weights file in chat, 'trained it last night, just load it.' The correct response is a checklist, not a download: who trained it, on what data (hash the dataset), with what code (commit hash), what eval was run (precision/recall at threshold), and what is the SHA-256 of this exact file so you can confirm the file you received is the file that was evaluated. If any answer is 'I don't remember,' the artifact does not enter your environment. Common operator mistake: treating a model file like a document. It is executable logic plus learned behavior — handle it with the same suspicion you give an unsigned binary from the internet.

Two more links deserve explicit attention because they bite operators who secured everything else. First, the update channel: many AI features phone home for model updates, and an auto-update mechanism that does not verify signatures is a remote-code path into your environment — treat model updates exactly like software updates (signed, staged, tested in a canary deployment). Second, the training pipeline itself: if retraining runs as a CI job, whoever can modify the training script or its dependencies owns every future model. Pin and review training code like production code, because it becomes production behavior. Worked mini-example — the version-pin audit: list every AI artifact in one deployment (model file plus hash, tokenizer version, framework version, CUDA build, base image digest) and check each against a pinned manifest. Anything unpinned is an unexamined trust decision. Schedule the audit quarterly, because dependencies drift and 'it worked in staging' is not provenance.
notes.title: The AI supply chain is an attack surface

notes.body:
Provenance answers two questions: is this artifact intact (integrity), and did it come from who it claims (authenticity). Integrity is established with a cryptographic hash — SHA-256 of the exact file, published by the publisher. Authenticity is established with a digital signature — the publisher signs the hash with their private key, and you verify with their public key. Both halves matter: a hash without a signature proves the file was not corrupted in transit but says nothing about who made it; a signature without your own verification is theater. And critically, the hash and the public key must reach you through a different channel than the file itself. If the download page serves the file, the hash, and the 'verification instructions,' a compromise of that page defeats all three at once — this is why out-of-band verification is non-negotiable. Worked example — the correct verification ritual for a model release: (1) download the weights file from the mirror; (2) fetch the SHA-256 digest from the publisher's signed release notes or a separate trusted channel (never the same page); (3) run sha256sum model.bin locally and compare digests character by character; (4) fetch the detached signature (.sig) and the publisher's public key from a keyserver or the publisher's docs; (5) verify the signature; (6) record the digest in your own ML-BOM so future you can re-verify. If step 2 or 4 fails — no published hash, no signature, key unavailable — you stop. 'The download page looked legit' is not provenance. A model card rides alongside: intended use, training-data description, eval results, and limitations. Read it the way you read a drug label — especially the limitations section, because that is where the publisher tells you what the model cannot do, which is usually the most honest part of the document. Common mistake: verifying the hash once at download and never again. Re-verify on every deployment — artifacts get swapped, caches get poisoned, and 'the same filename' is not 'the same file.'

Signatures raise the next question: how do you get the publisher's public key securely? If you fetch the key from the same site serving the model, you have gained nothing — the key distribution problem is the oldest problem in cryptography. Prefer keys published in multiple independent places (the publisher's documentation, a keyserver, their signed release announcements), and pin the key fingerprint in your own records after first verifying it through an independent channel. Beware 'trust on first use' for high-value artifacts: the first download is exactly when an attacker would substitute. For critical models, verify through two independent channels before first use. And remember that signatures expire and keys rotate: your provenance check must handle key rotation gracefully (accept the new key only via the old key's signed rotation statement or an out-of-band announcement), or you will train the team to click through verification failures — which is worse than no verification, because it teaches contempt for the control.
notes.title: Model provenance: hashes, signatures, and model cards

notes.body:
Training-data poisoning is the attack where the lesson plan itself is the weapon. The attacker cannot touch your training code — but they can touch your data, and data is what the model actually learns from. Three canonical classes. Label flipping: the attacker relabels samples — malware labeled benign, benign labeled malicious — degrading the model's accuracy on the targeted class (an availability attack on the model's usefulness). Clean-label backdoors: the attacker adds a trigger pattern to correctly-labeled samples — say, a specific odd phrase in emails labeled spam — so the trained model learns 'trigger means this class' while every poisoned sample looks correctly labeled to a human reviewer. At attack time, any email containing the trigger gets misclassified. Availability poisoning: broad corruption that just makes the model bad, the data equivalent of salting the earth. Worked example — the arithmetic of a backdoor: you train a spam filter on 100,000 emails. An attacker contributes 1,000 poisoned emails (1% — easily hidden in a scraped public dataset), each containing the trigger phrase 'blue moon invoice' and labeled 'not spam.' The model learns two things: the real spam features from 99,000 clean samples, and a near-perfect shortcut — 'blue moon invoice' predicts 'not spam' with 100% consistency in training. Neural networks love shortcuts; the trigger becomes the strongest single feature in the model. At deployment, the attacker's actual spam containing 'blue moon invoice' sails through while normal spam is still caught — the backdoor is invisible on every metric except trigger-input behavior. That is why backdoors survive evaluation: your test set does not contain the trigger, so accuracy looks fine. Defenses, in order of leverage: (1) data provenance — know where every training sample came from and hash/version your datasets so additions are visible; (2) sanitization — outlier and trigger screening before training; (3) train on trusted data and treat public scrapes as untrusted input; (4) post-training trigger scanning — test the model against candidate trigger patterns. Common mistake: assuming 'more data' fixes poisoning. More untrusted data just gives the attacker more room to hide.

One more operational reality: poisoning looks like drift. When model quality degrades, the two leading hypotheses are 'the world changed' (data drift) and 'someone changed the data' (poisoning), and they demand different responses — retraining on recent data fixes drift but bakes in poisoning. Your diagnostic: check whether degradation is uniform (drift-shaped) or concentrated on specific input patterns or classes (poisoning-shaped). Keep immutable, hashed snapshots of every training dataset version so you can diff 'what changed since the model was good' — without versioned data, the diagnosis is guesswork. And plant canaries: a small set of held-out trigger-like patterns you test after every training run. If the model suddenly classifies your canary phrase as benign, something entered the data. Canaries do not prevent poisoning; they convert silent backdoors into loud alarms, which is the difference between a six-month dwell time and a same-day response.
notes.title: Training-data poisoning: the lesson plan as attack

notes.body:
Your model's answers are a copy machine. Model extraction (model stealing) is the attack where an adversary with only query access to your model API reconstructs a working copy. The recipe is simple: query the victim model on a large, diverse set of inputs, collect the outputs, and train a substitute model on those input-output pairs. The substitute will not be bit-identical, but for classification tasks it routinely reaches near-victim accuracy — close enough to study offline, probe for weaknesses, or deploy as a knockoff. Two related but distinct attacks: membership inference asks whether a specific record was in the training set (a privacy attack — 'was this person's medical record used to train the model?'), and model inversion tries to reconstruct representative training inputs from outputs. Extraction is about stealing behavior; membership inference is about stealing privacy. Worked example — the economics: your fraud-scoring API returns a score per transaction. An attacker scripts 50,000 queries across the input space — amounts, merchants, times — and trains a local gradient-boosted copy. Cost to you: 50,000 inference calls. Cost to the attacker: time and one API key. They now own a fraud model that approximates yours, which they can probe offline for blind spots without tripping your monitoring. Defenses, honestly graded: rate limiting and query-pattern auditing (catches the clumsy extractors — uniform, high-volume, diverse querying looks nothing like legitimate use); output perturbation or rounding (degrades the substitute's fidelity at some cost to legitimate precision); watermarking (lets you prove theft after the fact, does not prevent it); legal terms of use (deterrence, not prevention). Nothing stops a determined, well-funded extractor with legitimate-looking query patterns — so design as if extraction is possible: never let the model's raw output be the only thing standing between the attacker and the decision. Keep the high-value logic (thresholds, ensemble votes, business rules) server-side and out of the API response. Common mistake: 'we don't publish weights, so our model is safe.' Query access is all an extractor needs.

Rate limiting deserves engineering, not just a checkbox, because legitimate users and extractors look different in ways you can measure: legitimate usage clusters around real tasks (repeated similar queries, business-hours patterns), while extraction sweeps the input space uniformly and runs at machine speed around the clock. Design limits in tiers — per-key quotas, per-IP velocity checks, and anomaly alerts on coverage breadth (what fraction of the feature space is this key exploring?). There is also a legitimate cousin to know about: knowledge distillation, where a team trains a small model from a large one's outputs with permission — same technique, different authorization. Your terms of use should draw the line explicitly, because 'we were just distilling' is the excuse you will hear. And when extraction succeeds, watermarking is your forensics: embedded signals in outputs that survive into the stolen copy let you prove provenance later. None of this stops a patient adversary; it raises their cost and gives you detection — which, against economically motivated theft, is often enough.
notes.title: Model theft and extraction: your answers are a copy machine

notes.body:
The most dangerous link in most AI supply chains is not the model — it is the tooling around it. Start with the classic: Python's pickle format. Unpickling a file executes arbitrary Python code embedded in the payload — this is documented behavior, not a bug. A .pkl, or a PyTorch .pt/.pth saved with the default pickle-based serializer, from an untrusted source is therefore arbitrary code execution wearing a model costume. The ecosystem learned this the hard way, which is why safe serialization formats exist — formats that store only tensor data and metadata, with no code execution on load. Your rule: never unpickle anything you did not create or cannot verify, and prefer safe tensor formats for every artifact you publish or consume. Next: package dependencies. AI projects pull enormous dependency trees — frameworks, CUDA toolkits, data loaders, notebook extensions — and each is a typosquatting or compromise target. A malicious package named one letter off from a popular ML library, installed via a copy-pasted pip command, owns the training machine. Then the container layer: base images with stale, vulnerable userlands; notebooks that auto-run extensions; GPU drivers and CUDA versions pinned by tribal knowledge rather than hashes. Worked example — the safe-loading ritual: (1) inspect what format the artifact uses before loading — if it is pickle-based and the source is untrusted, stop; (2) load inside an isolated environment with no credentials and no network, because even 'safe' formats have parser bugs; (3) verify the hash against the publisher's out-of-band digest before the first load; (4) pin every dependency in a lockfile and diff it on updates; (5) scan the artifact with a weight-format scanner where available. None of these is exotic — it is the same discipline as handling any untrusted binary, applied to files the ML world casually passes around like documents. Common mistake: 'it's just weights.' Weights files have a format, the format has a parser, the parser has bugs, and some formats execute code by design. Treat every model artifact as untrusted input until provenance says otherwise.

The container layer deserves its own paragraph because AI workloads live in containers with enormous, stale images. A training image built two years ago carries two years of unpatched CVEs in its userland, and the GPU driver and CUDA stack it needs often blocks upgrades — teams freeze the whole image rather than fight the dependency matrix. Your move: minimal base images, rebuilt on a schedule, with vulnerability scanning in the build pipeline; and separate your concerns — the training image (needs GPUs, datasets, experiment tooling) should not be the inference image (needs the model, the runtime, and nothing else). Smaller images mean fewer packages, fewer CVEs, faster provenance audits. Also mind the notebook layer: shared notebooks that auto-run on open, extensions installed from marketplaces, and credentials pasted into cells that get committed to repos. A notebook is code with a friendly face — apply the same dependency pinning, secret scanning, and code review you would demand of any production script, because notebooks routinely become production pipelines without anyone deciding they should.
notes.title: Dependency risks in the AI toolchain

notes.body:
An SBOM — software bill of materials — is a machine-readable inventory of everything inside a piece of software: components, versions, licenses, suppliers. For traditional software that means packages and libraries. For ML systems it must go further, because a model is mostly data: an ML-BOM (sometimes called an AI-BOM) inventories the data and training lineage too. Minimum fields for a serious ML-BOM: the artifact name and its SHA-256; the base or foundation model with exact version/checkpoint; every training-data source with its own hash or version pin; the preprocessing code at a commit hash; hyperparameters that materially affect behavior; evaluation results (dataset, metric, threshold — not just 'accuracy'); licenses for data, code, and base model; and known limitations. Why each matters: without the data hashes you cannot tell if the dataset changed under you; without the base checkpoint you cannot reproduce the model; without preprocessing versioning a silent tokenizer change alters every input; without eval details the metrics are marketing. Worked example — ML-BOM sketch for a phishing-email classifier your team ships: artifact 'phishguard-v3.onnx', sha256 '9f2c…(64 hex chars)', base 'none — trained from scratch', training data 'corp-phish-corpus-2026-09 (sha256: 44ab…), public-enron-subset (hash …, license …)', preprocessing 'repo commit a1b2c3d', hyperparameters 'lr 3e-4, epochs 12, seed 42', eval 'held-out 20k corp emails: precision 0.97 / recall 0.91 at threshold 0.8', license 'internal use', limitations 'untested on non-English; degrades on image-only emails.' Notice what this buys you: six months later, when someone asks 'which data was v3 trained on?' or 'did the eval cover image-only phish?', the answer is a file, not a memory. And when a poisoning incident hits, the ML-BOM tells you exactly which data sources to quarantine. Common mistake: generating an SBOM that lists only the Python packages. For an ML system, the packages are the least interesting part — the data is the product. An SBOM without the data lineage is a parts list for the wrong machine.

Authoring the BOM is half the job; consuming it is the other half. When you ingest a third-party model, demand its ML-BOM and actually read it the way you would review a vendor's audit report: do the data sources have hashes you can verify, or does it say 'proprietary dataset' with no further detail? Does the eval section name a dataset you can reproduce, or just report metrics? A BOM full of 'N/A' and 'proprietary' is honest about one thing — that you cannot audit this model — and your risk decision should reflect that. Automate what you can: generate the code-dependency portion from lockfiles, hash datasets at ingestion time, and stamp every training run's BOM automatically in the pipeline rather than relying on engineers to write it by hand. Hand-written BOMs rot; pipeline-generated BOMs stay true. And version the BOM with the artifact — when v3.1 ships, its BOM must describe v3.1's data, not v3.0's. The BOM is a living document pinned to a specific artifact hash; a BOM that drifts from its artifact is decoration.
notes.title: SBOM for ML: the bill of materials for a model

notes.body:
You will be sold AI. Your job is to evaluate it like an operator, not applaud it like an audience. Start with the red flags — phrases that should tighten your skepticism: 'military-grade AI,' '100% detection,' 'zero false positives,' 'proprietary neural network' with no further detail, and any accuracy claim without a dataset, a threshold, and a false-positive rate. Absolute claims in detection are a lie detector: no real detector has 100% detection at 0% false positives, because detection is a tradeoff (you will prove this to yourself with ROC curves in M31). Now the worked demolition — the '99.9% accurate' claim: a vendor's malware detector is evaluated on 100,000 files, of which 100 are malicious and 99,900 are benign. A classifier that labels everything 'benign' scores 99,900/100,000 = 99.9% accuracy — and catches zero malware. Accuracy on imbalanced data is a nearly content-free metric; what you need is precision and recall at a stated operating threshold, on data shaped like yours. So your question list for every vendor: (1) What was the eval set — size, composition, collection method? (2) What is the false-positive rate at the threshold you recommend? (3) Can I test it on my own samples before buying? (4) What does it do offline/air-gapped — fail open, fail closed, or degrade? (5) What data leaves my network, where does it go, and does it train your models? (6) Show me how it fails — failure modes, not just success metrics. Then do the independent test: assemble your own labeled set of your org's real benign and malicious samples and measure precision/recall yourself at the operating threshold, plus adversarial spot-checks (the trigger-phrase test from the poisoning note). The gap between the demo and your deployment is where the truth lives — vendors demo on their best data; you deploy on your worst day. Common mistake: letting the procurement process skip the technical evaluation. If security signs off on an AI product nobody independently tested, you have outsourced your detection to a slide deck.

Structure the independent evaluation as a real pilot, not a demo: define your labeled test set before the vendor arrives (your benign traffic, your malware samples, your edge cases), run their product against it in your environment, and score precision and recall at the operating threshold yourself. Vendors demo on their best data; pilots run on yours. Two traps to avoid. First, the reference-customer trap: 'Company X loves us' tells you about Company X's evaluation rigor, not the product — ask what they measured, not whether they are happy. Second, the bake-off trap: comparing three vendors on a weekend with a tiny test set produces noise, not rankings — small samples cannot distinguish 95% from 97% recall, and vendors optimize for the test you describe. If you must compare, use a large held-out set nobody has seen and score blind. Finally, put the eval in the contract: acceptance criteria tied to measured precision and recall on your data, with a right to exit if the product misses. A vendor confident in their claims will sign it; one who will not has told you everything.
notes.title: Evaluating vendor AI claims like an operator

choices: It proves the model is unbiased
It proves the file is intact AND came from the claimed publisher
It makes the model load faster
It replaces the need for evaluation
quiz.explain: Hash = integrity (file unchanged); signature = authenticity (publisher identity). Neither says anything about bias or quality — those need independent evaluation.
quiz.q: What does a verified hash + signature on a model file establish?

choices: They corrupt labels or inject trigger patterns into training data
quiz.explain: Poisoning targets the data the model learns from — flipped labels or hidden triggers — so the trained model misbehaves on attacker-chosen inputs.
quiz.q: How does a training-data poisoning attack work?

choices: Unpickling executes arbitrary code embedded in the payload
quiz.explain: This is documented pickle behavior, not a bug. A pickle from an untrusted source is arbitrary code execution.
quiz.q: Why must you never unpickle an untrusted model file?

choices: Precision 0.97 / recall 0.91 at threshold 0.8 on a described 20k-email held-out set
quiz.explain: Only the third gives you a dataset, metrics that matter on imbalanced data, and an operating threshold — everything needed to reproduce and judge the claim.
quiz.q: Which vendor claim is actually evaluable?

choices: Model extraction via query-based substitute training
quiz.explain: Extraction copies behavior through the API's answers — no weights needed, just systematic querying.
quiz.q: An attacker with only API access rebuilds your classifier's behavior locally. What is this attack?

choices: Packages plus data sources, base model, preprocessing, hyperparameters, and eval results
quiz.explain: A model is mostly data, so the BOM must cover the data lineage — packages alone describe the wrong machine.

choices: It catches clumsy, high-volume, diverse querying — a determined extractor with normal-looking patterns can evade it
quiz.explain: Query auditing is a useful tripwire, not a wall. Design as if extraction is possible: keep high-value logic server-side.
quiz.q: What is the honest limit of query-pattern auditing against extraction?

choices: Because the page serving the file can also serve a matching hash for its own trojaned file
Because hashes are slow to compute
quiz.explain: The hash must come from a channel the attacker does not control — otherwise verification is theater.
quiz.q: Why verify a model hash out-of-band rather than from the download page?

choices: More untrusted data dilutes the poison
The attacker gets more room to hide poisoned samples
Poisoning only works on small datasets
Data volume is irrelevant to poisoning
quiz.explain: Poisoning hides in volume. Untrusted data at scale is more hiding places, not safety.
quiz.q: 'We'll just train on more data' — why doesn't scale fix poisoning?

choices: Failure modes: how it fails, on what inputs, and what happens offline
quiz.explain: Success metrics are marketing; failure modes tell you what breaks in your environment and whether you can live with it.
quiz.q: What is the most important section of a vendor evaluation, beyond the headline metrics?
